stem: An indirect tax on a good is represented on a diagram by a shift of

options.content: the supply curve upward by the amount of the tax
options.rationale: Correct: the tax raises costs.

options.content: the demand curve upward by the amount of the tax
options.rationale: Demand does not shift; the tax is collected from sellers.

options.content: the demand curve to the left
options.rationale: A tax on sellers shifts supply, not demand.

options.content: the supply curve to the right
options.rationale: A subsidy shifts supply to the right.

explanation: The tax raises the sellers' cost of each unit, so the supply curve shifts upward (to the left) by the amount of the tax.

stem: The incidence of an indirect tax refers to

options.content: how the burden is shared between consumers and producers
options.rationale: Correct: who really pays.

options.content: the amount of revenue the government receives
options.rationale: That is the tax revenue.

options.content: the fall in the quantity traded
options.rationale: That is the effect on quantity.

options.content: the size of the subsidy
options.rationale: That concerns subsidies.

explanation: Incidence is how the burden of the tax is shared between consumers and producers.

stem: A subsidy paid to producers of a good will

options.content: raise the price and lower the quantity traded
options.rationale: That follows a tax.

options.content: lower the price and lower the quantity traded
options.rationale: A subsidy raises quantity.

options.content: leave the price unchanged
options.rationale: The price falls when supply increases.

options.content: lower the price and raise the quantity traded
options.rationale: Correct: supply shifts to the right.

explanation: A subsidy lowers costs, shifting supply to the right: the equilibrium price falls and quantity rises.

stem: When demand for a good is inelastic and supply is elastic, an indirect tax is borne

options.content: mostly by producers
options.rationale: That happens when demand is elastic and supply is inelastic.

options.content: mostly by consumers
options.rationale: Correct: they keep buying at the higher price.

options.content: equally by consumers and producers
options.rationale: Equal sharing needs equal elasticities.

options.content: entirely by the government
options.rationale: The government collects the tax.

explanation: The more inelastic side bears more of the burden: consumers cannot easily cut back, so they pay most of the tax.
hints: Which side finds it harder to avoid the tax?

stem: A tax of US\$5 per unit reduces the quantity sold from 600 to 520. Tax revenue is

options.rationale: This uses the old quantity.
This is the quantity, not the revenue.
This is the fall in quantity.
Correct: tax per unit × new quantity.

explanation: Revenue = 5 × 520 = US\$2,600. The old quantity is not used because 80 units are no longer sold.
hints: Revenue = tax per unit × quantity after the tax.

stem: A government wants to raise as much revenue as possible from an indirect tax. It should tax a good that has

options.content: elastic demand
options.rationale: Quantity falls sharply and revenue is lower.

options.content: many close substitutes
options.rationale: Consumers switch away and revenue falls.

options.content: inelastic demand
options.rationale: Correct: consumption is little reduced.

options.content: perfectly elastic demand
options.rationale: Quantity would fall to zero.

explanation: With inelastic demand quantity falls little, so revenue is high.
hints: Which goods have the smallest fall in quantity?

stem: An economist says a subsidy creates a welfare loss. This means that

options.content: producers earn less profit because the subsidy lowers the price they receive
options.rationale: Producers receive more per unit.

options.content: the cost to the government exceeds the gain in consumer and producer surplus
options.rationale: Correct: some output is worth less than it costs.

options.content: the quantity traded falls because the subsidy raises the price consumers pay
options.rationale: A subsidy raises quantity.

options.content: consumers pay a higher price for the good because of the subsidy
options.rationale: The price falls.

explanation: The subsidy encourages output beyond the equilibrium: the extra units cost more to produce than their value to consumers, and the cost to the government exceeds the gain in surplus.

stem: Which is the strongest criticism of a high indirect tax on a necessity with inelastic demand?

options.content: It reduces consumption by a very large amount among all households
options.rationale: With inelastic demand quantity falls little.

options.content: It raises no revenue because demand is inelastic
options.rationale: Revenue is high when demand is inelastic.

options.content: It hits poorer households hard but cuts consumption little
options.rationale: Correct: regressive and ineffective at changing behaviour.

options.content: Producers bear the whole of the tax because supply is elastic
options.rationale: Consumers bear most of it when demand is inelastic.

explanation: Poor households spend a larger share of their income on necessities, so the tax is regressive and may not reduce consumption much.
hints: Think about who pays and the elasticities.

stem: A market has demand P = 40 − 0.04Q and supply P = 8 + 0.04Q (P in US\$, Q in units). A tax of US\$4 per unit is imposed on sellers. Calculate the new equilibrium price paid by consumers.
explanation: The tax shifts supply to P = 12 + 0.04Q. Then 40 − 0.04Q = 12 + 0.04Q, so 28 = 0.08Q, Q = 350 and P = 40 − 14 = US\$26. (Before the tax: US\$24 and 400 units.)
workedSolution: 1. The tax shifts supply to P = 12 + 0.04Q. Then 40 − 0.04Q = 12 + 0.04Q, so 28 = 0.08Q, Q = 350 and P = 40 − 14 = US\$26. (Before the tax: US\$24 and 400 units.)

stem: In the same market (a tax of US\$4 per unit; the quantity after the tax is 350 units) calculate the government's tax revenue.
explanation:
1. Tax per unit = US\$4.
2. Quantity sold after the tax = 350.
3. Revenue = 4 × 350 = US\$1,400. Using the old quantity (400) gives 1,600.
workedSolution:
1. 1. Tax per unit = US\$4.
2. Quantity sold after the tax = 350.
3. Revenue = 4 × 350 = US\$1,400. Using the old quantity (400) gives 1,600.
hints: Use the quantity after the tax.

stem: In the same market the tax of US\$4 per unit reduces the quantity from 400 to 350. Calculate the deadweight loss.
explanation: Deadweight loss = ½ × 4 × (400 − 350) = US\$100. Forgetting the half gives 200.
workedSolution: 1. Deadweight loss = ½ × 4 × (400 − 350) = US\$100. Forgetting the half gives 200.
hints: The deadweight loss is a triangle: ½ × tax × fall in quantity.

stem: In the same market (demand P = 40 − 0.04Q, supply P = 8 + 0.04Q) the government pays a subsidy of US\$4 per unit to sellers. The new supply is P = 4 + 0.04Q. Calculate the cost of the subsidy to the government.
explanation: New equilibrium: 40 − 0.04Q = 4 + 0.04Q, so Q = 450 and P = US\$22. Cost = 4 × 450 = US\$1,800. Using the old quantity (400) gives 1,600.
workedSolution: 1. New equilibrium: 40 − 0.04Q = 4 + 0.04Q, so Q = 450 and P = US\$22. Cost = 4 × 450 = US\$1,800. Using the old quantity (400) gives 1,600.
hints: Cost = subsidy per unit × new quantity.

stem: A good sells at US\$20 before tax. An ad valorem tax of 15% of the pre-tax price is imposed and the whole tax is passed on to the consumer. Calculate the price the consumer pays.
explanation: Tax = 15% × 20 = US\$3, so the consumer pays US\$23. Adding 15 instead of 15% gives 35.
workedSolution: 1. Tax = 15% × 20 = US\$3, so the consumer pays US\$23. Adding 15 instead of 15% gives 35.

stem: If demand is perfectly inelastic, consumers bear the whole of an indirect tax.
explanation: True. Quantity does not change, so the price rises by the full amount of the tax.

stem: Match each market condition with who bears most of an indirect tax.
explanation: The more inelastic side of the market bears more of the tax.

stem: What name is given to the way the burden of a tax is shared between consumers and producers?
explanation: Tax incidence.

stem: Distinguish between a specific tax and an ad valorem tax.

points.description: A specific tax is a fixed amount per unit.
An ad valorem tax is a percentage of the price.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A specific tax is a fixed sum charged on each unit, such as US\$4 per litre. An ad valorem tax is a percentage of the price, such as 15%, so the tax per unit rises with the price.

explanation: Fixed amount against percentage of price.

stem: Explain the effect of an indirect tax on the equilibrium price and quantity of a good.

points.description: The tax raises sellers' costs by the amount of the tax.
Supply shifts upward (to the left).
Equilibrium price rises.
Equilibrium quantity falls (by an amount that depends on elasticity).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: An indirect tax raises the cost of supplying each unit by the amount of the tax, so the supply curve shifts upward or to the left. At the old price there is excess demand, so the equilibrium price rises and the equilibrium quantity falls, by more if demand and supply are elastic.

explanation: Cost rise, supply shift, new price and quantity.
hints: Describe the shift, the price and the quantity.

stem: Analyse why consumers bear most of a tax on cigarettes.

points.description: Demand for cigarettes is inelastic (addiction, few substitutes).
Consumers keep buying despite the price rise, so quantity falls little.
Sellers can pass most of the tax on in a higher price.
Therefore consumers' share of the burden is greater than producers'.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Demand for cigarettes is inelastic because many smokers are addicted and there are few close substitutes. When the tax raises the supply price, consumers keep buying, so quantity falls only slightly and sellers can pass most of the tax on in a higher price. Consumers therefore bear a larger share of the burden than producers.

explanation: Inelastic demand shifts incidence to consumers.
hints: Use the relative elasticity of demand and supply.

stem: A fictional market for cooking oil has demand P = 30 − 0.05Q and supply P = 6 + 0.05Q (P in US\$ per bottle, Q in bottles per week). The equilibrium is a price of US\$18 and 240 bottles. The government imposes a tax of US\$6 per bottle on sellers, so that supply becomes P = 12 + 0.05Q.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the total amount of the tax borne by consumers.
parts.explanation: Consumers pay US\$3 more per bottle (21 − 18): 3 × 180 = US\$540.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Consumers pay US\$3 more per bottle (21 − 18): 3 × 180 = US\$540.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why producers bear part of the tax.

points.description: The price rises by only US\$3 of the US\$6 tax.
Producers receive US\$15 per bottle after paying the tax, US\$3 less than before (and sell fewer bottles).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The price paid by consumers rises by only US\$3, half of the tax, so sellers keep only US\$15 of the US\$21 after paying the US\$6 tax, which is US\$3 less than the US\$18 they received before. They also sell fewer bottles.

explanation: Price 18 → 21, quantity 240 → 180, revenue 1,080, shared equally; deadweight loss 180.
hints: The supply curve moves up by the tax.

stem: A fictional government pays farmers a subsidy of US\$8 per tonne of maize. Before the subsidy, demand is P = 50 − 0.1Q and supply is P = 10 + 0.1Q (P in US\$ per tonne, Q in tonnes), giving a price of US\$30 and 200 tonnes. With the subsidy, supply is P = 2 + 0.1Q.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the new price paid by consumers.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the cost of the subsidy to the government.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate how much of the subsidy payment benefits consumers through the lower price (fall in price per tonne × quantity after the subsidy).
parts.explanation: The price falls by US\$4 (30 to 26): 4 × 240 = US\$960.
parts.workedSolution: 1. The price falls by US\$4 (30 to 26): 4 × 240 = US\$960.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why the subsidy creates a welfare loss.

points.description: It encourages output beyond the equilibrium of 200 tonnes (to 240).
The extra 40 tonnes cost more to produce than their value to consumers, so the cost to the government exceeds the gain in surplus (by US\$160).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The subsidy raises output from 200 to 240 tonnes. The extra tonnes cost more to produce than consumers value them, so the subsidy costs the government US\$1,920 but raises consumer and producer surplus by only US\$1,760: a welfare loss of US\$160.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State **one** drawback of the subsidy and explain it.

points.description: Cost to taxpayers (or opportunity cost of the funds), or dependence or inefficiency, or the benefit goes mostly to larger farmers.
Explanation linked to the data or to the effect on behaviour.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: One drawback is the cost: US\$1,920 of public money is used, which could have been spent on other things such as roads or schools, and farmers may become dependent on the support.

explanation: Price 30 → 26, quantity 200 → 240, cost 1,920, welfare loss 160.
hints: The supply curve moves down by the subsidy.
Cost = subsidy per unit × new quantity.

stem: Assess whether an indirect tax is an effective way to reduce the consumption of tobacco.

points.description: A tax raises price and reduces quantity demanded.
Demand for tobacco is inelastic (addiction), so the fall in consumption is small.
Tax revenue is high and can fund health care or education.
The tax is regressive: poor smokers pay a bigger share of income.
Smuggling and illegal trade reduce effectiveness.
Long-run demand is more elastic, especially for young people.
Alternatives: information, advertising bans, regulation.
A justified judgement.

levels.descriptor: Two-sided, applied and developed, with a justified conclusion.
Some development of one or both sides, limited application or conclusion.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: An indirect tax raises the price of tobacco and so reduces the quantity demanded. However, demand for tobacco is inelastic because many smokers are addicted and there are few substitutes, so the tax reduces consumption by only a small amount, though it raises substantial revenue that can fund health care. The tax is regressive, since poorer smokers pay a larger share of their income, and high taxes can encourage smuggling. In the long run, and for young people who are not yet addicted, demand is more elastic, so the effect is greater. Overall a tax is effective at raising revenue and moderately effective at reducing consumption, and it works best alongside information campaigns and regulation.

explanation: Tax effect limited by inelastic demand; distribution and alternatives; judgement.
